events.excerpt: More than 1,600 Rockstar Games employees in the UK will begin voting on union recognition on Thursday, with the ballot kicking off just a week before the long-awaited launch of Grand Theft Auto VI. The ballot, which opens on November 12 and runs until November 26, will determine whether Rockstar formally recognizes the Rockstar Game Workers Union, part of the Independent Workers Union of Great Britain (IWGB). Nearly all UK employees below director level are eligible to vote. If successful, the union would become the largest recognized union in the UK games industry, giving workers a collective voice. The proposed recognition agreement follows four months of negotiations between Rockstar management and employees. It would allow workers to negotiate over pay, overtime, pensions, bonuses, leave and other employment conditions, while securing consultation rights over HR policies and AI. The vote comes at a particularly busy time for Rockstar, with GTA VI finally due to arrive on November 19, more than 13 years after its predecessor. The game is expected to be one of the biggest entertainment launches in history, although the people responsible for making it have rather more immediate concerns than sales records. events.excerpt: A new extension brings a working global menu bar to the GNOME desktop, even for some apps that don’t have menu bars at all. Orbit Global Menu is a new GNOME extension that gives the GNOME desktop a feature it was intentionally designed without, and one that some users miss very badly – this vulture being one of them. It adds a working global menu bar to the GNOME top panel. We suspect this is something that will cause strongly contrasting opinions among many GNOME users: some will by puzzled why anyone would bother, while others may think "at last!" and rush to try it. There have been other attempts to do this before, and the Reg FOSS desk has tried several of them, but we never found one that worked with the majority of applications. Our fondness for this UI feature was visible in the two-part series we wrote in September on how to customize Xfce and then in part two how to get the global menu working with more apps. The problem is getting worse over time, as in recent versions (since GNOME 40 and Gtk4), the GNOME human-interface guidelines encourage smartphone-style hamburger menus, replacing the traditional horizontal menu bar. events.excerpt: Welcome, once again, to PWNED, where all the victims are self-owned. This week, we welcome you to a London hotel where you could check out its admin credentials for a booking website just by walking past the front desk. Our story comes courtesy of Neycho Tepavicharov, co-founder of Flashcloud, a Delaware-based web hosting company. He was staying at a hotel in London when he noticed a shocking breach of basic security protocols by management, who were a little too hospitable with their credentials. As he was passing through the lobby, Tepavicharov noticed that the door behind the front desk was open and, inside that back room, there was a whiteboard. On the whiteboard, written in plain English, were the hotel’s Booking.com administrative username and password. Anyone near the desk could clearly see the login information, and if they didn’t have time to write it down, they could have snapped a picture for later use. As Tepavicharov explains, there’s plenty of mischief you could perform with these credentials. “With that login, someone could change or cancel reservations, see guests’ names and contact details, or message guests pretending to be the hotel,” he said. “Fake 'please confirm your payment' messages sent from compromised hotel accounts are a well-known scam.” An attacker c

events.excerpt: I would like to discuss a wallet design built around three components: Lindell 2-of-2 MPC signing, QR-only initialization, and encrypted NFC communication between a computer and a phone. The goal is to keep the convenience of a desktop wallet while ensuring that compromising either device alone does not provide unilateral signing authority. Lindell 2-of-2 MPC as the signing foundation The computer and phone each hold a private share of one joint signing key. Neither device holds the complete private key. Using a reviewed implementation of Lindell’s two-party ECDSA protocol , both devices interact to compute a signature without revealing their shares or reconstructing the complete private key. For Ethereum, the implementation would use secp256k1 and produce one ordinary ECDSA signature under the joint public key. The wallet can therefore use a normal Ethereum address without requiring an on-chain multisignature contract. The 2-of-2 requirement comes from the signing protocol itself: obtaining the computer’s share alone is insufficient, and obtaining the phone’s share alone is also insufficient. Both devices must participate in signing the same transaction. Initialize entirely through QR codes Initialization takes place before connecting the NFC reader. Each device generates its ow

events.excerpt: Keeping sensitive data within national borders might satisfy a residency requirement. But does it mean your organization is genuinely in control? Not necessarily. Data could be stored locally while remaining subject to another jurisdiction's laws, dependent on overseas service providers or exposed to disruption beyond your control. For enterprise IT teams, that distinction is becoming harder to ignore. Geopolitical tensions, evolving regulations and the growing use of AI are forcing organizations to reconsider what data sovereignty means in practice. Yet translating those concerns into a workable strategy is another matter. And simply throwing more money at the problem won't necessarily solve it. In The Register's on-demand webinar, Data Sovereignty By Design, moderator Tim Phillips speaks with Patrick Smith, Field CTO for EMEA at Everpure, formerly Pure Storage, about moving beyond compliance checklists and taking a more strategic approach to data control. Drawing on findings from Everpure's research, Smith explores a curious disconnect: organizations are increasing their investment in sovereignty initiatives, yet many still lack a coordinated strategy. Some of the risks attracting the most attention aren't necessarily those receiving the greatest investment. The discussion exam
events.headline: Data sovereignty takes more than keeping data close to home

events.excerpt: Every so often a flaw comes along that shows how fast the ground can shift under IT and security teams. PHP2Shell, a pair of critical flaws in PHP, was one of them. Details leaked before the planned disclosure, frontier AI helped researchers find the flaws, and PHP shipped fixes the next day. For many teams, though, the patch was the easy part. So what does it take to respond at that speed, and where should teams begin? What does governed autonomous IT look like in practice? Picture a loop. Software finds where a risk lives and ranks what matters most. It proposes a fix, then, inside limits people define, carries it out and checks that it worked. Routine, low-risk actions can run on their own. Higher-impact ones wait for a person to approve. A few are never handed over at all. Each step leaves a record that someone can review and reverse. What challenges do IT and security teams face today? Three problems keep coming up. The first is visibility. PHP2Shell reportedly sat undetected for more than a decade. For these two flaws, the fix was a version upgrade. The hard part was finding every copy of PHP, including copies bundled inside other software or extracted by hand onto Windows machines that never registered as installed applications. events.excerpt: Disclosure: I am the creator of Atomic Ownership Blockchains (AOB), which this repo covers in more detail than the other designs. What this is An open-source skill (SKILL.md format, Apache-2.0) that lets LLM agents analyze blockchain architectures on several independent dimensions instead of one number. The Nakamoto coefficient is a single-subsystem snapshot, goes stale, and is not comparable across consensus mechanisms, so the skill treats it as one input per subsystem, not a ranking. Dimensions currently covered: Node/validator concentration (NC per subsystem), stake/wealth concentration (Gini/HHI), client diversity, network/infrastructure Consensus dependency scope: does finalizing this transaction need agreement from parties unrelated to it? Privileged actors, payment finality authority, reliance on economic assumptions Sybil exposure, blast radius of one attack or one lost key, eclipse/network-view attacks, cost to participate It compares PoW, PoS, DAG, sharded designs and AOB, and reports each design’s validation level (production history, audits, testnet) separately from what its architecture does. events.excerpt: AWS has released an emulator that kind-of-almost lets you use its cloud on a PC. As explained in the GitHub repository for the prosaically named “AWS Emulator,” the tool “is a local program that serves an AWS API endpoint.” The emulator doesn’t replicate the whole AWS cloud, instead offering its APIs. “You use it to test your software without calling AWS, on your own machine, on a development server, or in continuous integration (CI),” the repo explains. Because those tests never touch the AWS cloud, the tool is free to use. AWS wrote the emulator in Rust, a choice that senior specialist solutions architect Daniel Abib wrote helps to ensure the tool “stays light on CPU and memory on a laptop.” The emulator tool doesn’t replicate the entire AWS cloud. Abib said it supports the APIs of AWS services that have an API model in the AWS API models repository on GitHub . The Register found over 1,300 items on that page. While the tool lets developers test APIs, it doesn’t replicate anywhere near all the features of the Amazonian cloud. “It doesn’t evaluate IAM [Identity and Access Management] policies the way AWS does, and each emulator acts as a single account, with no cross-account or cross-Region behavior,” Abib wrote, adding “How closely it matches AWS varies by service and feature.”
events.headline: AWS distills its cloud into a local emulator that runs on your PC

events.excerpt: Former certification authority eMudhra has claimed a buggy Python script is the main reason it issued laughably insecure digital certificates. The company posted its account of the matter on Bugzilla where a user with the handle “Naveen Kumar ML” wrote “During a single key‑generation ceremony on 30 April 2025, sixteen subordinate (issuing) CA key pairs in eMudhra’s ‘B’ and ‘C’ series were generated correctly on a hardware security module and then processed through an approved wrap/unwrap round‑trip using a custom python key‑handling script.” eMudhra aimed to create eight ECDSA P-384 private keys which should have been 48 bytes long. But the script contained what Kumar described as “a bug/defect in the import code [which] resulted in a read‑back from the unwrapped object that truncated the private value, so the certified public keys correspond to private scalars below the expected range and are recoverable from public information.” The truncation is the key problem here, because it appears that eMudhra ignored 47 of the 48 bytes, producing its infamously insecure single-byte keys such as the number four. events.excerpt: Russian cloud operator Yandex has admitted to data loss after a drone attack on one of its datacenters. The attack, which Ukrainian press said was ordered by Kyiv, happened in early October and caused a fire and subsequent outage at Yandex’s ru-central1-b availability zone. Subsequent strikes targeted more Yandex datacenters and disrupted more of the company’s cloud and payment services. On Tuesday, Yandex posted an update on its recovery efforts, which it spun as something of a triumph because it restored over 97 percent of customer data. Of course that also means the company lost 2.84 percent of customer data, which it blamed on “critical hardware damage and a lack of backups on the platform.” It’s unclear if Yandex’s use of the phrase “on the platform” indicates it doesn’t keep backups of its own cloud, if whatever resilience techniques it employs don’t create multiple copies of customer data, or if clients didn’t protect their data. Whatever happened, Yandex has decided to enable backups by default for all VMs customers create in its cloud. That decision will mean customers will consume and pay for more Yandex resources, unless they opt out of the automated backups. events.excerpt: TL;DR A contract on Base checks every Zcash block header against Zcash’s consensus rules: the Equihash (200, 9) solution on the EIP-152 BLAKE2b precompile, the difficulty adjustment (including NU7’s 25-second blocks), the time rules and cumulative work. Contracts can then read Zcash’s best chain without trusting a bridge, a committee or whoever relays. Anyone can feed it; a feeder can delay the relay but cannot make it accept a header Zcash’s rules reject. One header costs about 626k gas (mean, whole transaction); Equihash is 361k of it. Following Zcash at 25-second blocks is ~3,456 headers, ≈ 2.2 × 10⁹ gas a day: about 0.01 ETH a day at Base’s 0.005 gwei. A relay deployed with Mainnet parameters on 29 October 2026 crossed Zcash Mainnet’s NU7 activation (height 3,543,405, 6 November 2026) without a redeploy and followed the 5,405 headers after it. On top of the relay: a RISC Zero proof (Groth16-wrapped, 256,720 gas to verify on Base) that a shielded payment of at least an amount went to a receiver an app committed to, with a memo naming the app’s reference, inside the ZIP 221 chain history of a header the relay holds. The transaction id, the note, the block and the address never reach the EVM chain. A real Testnet payment was proven in 81 s on a rented RTX 4090, for about one cen
events.headline: Seam: verifying Zcash headers on Base with EIP-152, and proving shielded payments without linking the chains

events.excerpt: This is Ethlabs’ view on post-quantum and post-AI timelines and how we think Ethereum’s protocol layer should prioritize them, after spending a week with coredevs at Devcon. tl;dr We think Ethereum can become post-quantum and (plausibly) post-AI in 2027: pqai27. This will future-proof Ethereum’s leading position as the credible decentralized root of trust for the global economy, with ETH as the programmable store of value at its center. Being post-quantum is not enough, we intend on being post-AI too. AI capabilities are taking off: quantum timelines are moving forward, AI is solving open maths problems that pose the question whether some cryptographic primitives might break, and it’s finding software vulnerabilities at scale. Ethereum is uniquely positioned for this moment and leading the way : years of prior research and work have produced a clear plan to become post-quantum and plausibly post-AI, and now we should make it the priority. The network is resilient through its decentralized validator set and client diversity, and formal verification is already deeply embedded into its core development process. pqai27 means rethinking upcoming hardforks , including Hegotá: anything not on the critical path to pqai should be reconsidered. events.excerpt: T-Mobile violated a New York state law by imposing a 50GB-per-month data cap and reducing speeds to less than a megabit per second on home Internet plans it is required to offer people with low incomes, New York government officials alleged. T-Mobile agreed to a settlement requiring it to scrap the data and speed limits, to offer the required low-income plans to more parts of the state, and to make it easier for customers to find information about the plans. The settlement requires T-Mobile to eliminate the speed limits and expand availability of the plans within 120 days. The alleged legal violation and the settlement are related to T-Mobile's wireless home Internet service, not the company's mobile plans. Governor Kathy Hochul and New York Attorney General Letitia James announced the settlement on Monday, saying that a state investigation found T-Mobile violated the New York Affordable Broadband Act (ABA). events.excerpt: Anduril Industries has announced the successful demonstration of a new satellite-based sensor designed to track other spacecraft that may be hiding their maneuvers in Earth's shadow. Funded with Anduril's internal capital, the company's oven-sized satellite launched on a SpaceX rideshare mission in July with a package of tech demo payloads: an edge-compute processor, a power-management system adaptable to different mission types, and a long-wave infrared space sensor capable of detecting other objects in orbit. Anduril reported on the success of the tech demo mission Tuesday. The company's satellite, named Anduril-216, flies about 590 km (366 mi) above Earth, spending about one-third of each orbit in darkness. Anduril-216's night passes allow its infrared imager to shine. events.excerpt: This release brings various stability improvements, ECDSA TX-form binding, and improved replica 2.9 syncing. We recommend installing it as soon as you can to address potential node stability issues. Configuration Note: the first time you start the node after upgrading to N.2.9.8, do not use the start_from_local_state or start_from_block configuration options. Syncing: Syncing could slow down to the pace of the slowest peer, even when much faster peers were available. Each storage module limits how much sync work it keeps in progress at once. When the node reached data that only a slow peer had, that peer's requests could take up the whole limit, and the node stopped moving on to the rest of the data. The faster peers that had the rest sat idle until the slow peer was done, which could take days. Restarts made this more likely. The node kept its sync position in memory only, so after a restart every storage module started over from the beginning. If the first missing data there was only available from slow peers, the storage module synced at their pace. We reproduced both cases in the sync simulator and fixed them: A single peer can now take up at most half of a storage module's sync work limit. The node puts aside the data that peer cannot take yet and comes back to it every seco

events.excerpt: A group of privacy enthusiasts discovered on Tuesday that the default software development kit (SDK) that wallet apps use to connect to Ledger hardware devices transmits details regarding crypto transaction signatures to Ledger servers. When the discovery spread on social media, privacy proponents were surprised to discover that Ledger crypto wallet apps have been quietly broadcasting transaction details to Ledger. The behavior has been a default since Ledger’s context-module version 1.16, i.e. since May 2026 or earlier. It was a devastating discovery for users who have mistakenly thought the default behavior of Ledger wallets was private signing and private broadcasts of transactions directly to blockchain networks. Unfortunately, many Ledger wallets have been simultaneously doxxing personal details to the world’s largest hardware wallet manufacturer. Substantial metadata has been transmitting from Ledger devices to Ledger servers since late May. Apps and users must opt-out of this information-sharing behavior when using wallet apps, and the overwhelming majority do not.
